This worksheet rebuilds the models of the
[lecture on regression analysis](/content/lecture/l_10_Regression.qmd) in R,
on exactly the same data, and in the same order: first a simple regression
through all six steps of a regression analysis (question, explore, specify,
estimate, diagnose, interpret), then multiple regression, then groups and
interactions. Every number quoted in the lecture appears somewhere below.

# Setup

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(tidyverse)  # readr, dplyr, ggplot2, purrr
library(broom)      # tidy(), glance(), augment()
```

```{r}
#| label: fmt
#| include: false

# numbers in the text: fixed decimals, typographic minus
fmt <- function(x, d = 0) sub("-", "\u2212", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))
```

```{r}
#| label: load-data-shown
#| eval: false

cps <- read_csv("cps-earnings-mra-2014.csv")
```

```{r}
#| label: load-data
#| echo: false
#| message: false

cps <- read_csv("../data/cps-earnings-mra-2014.csv")
```

```{r}
#| label: prepare-data

cps <- cps |>
  mutate(
    female  = as.integer(sex == 2),
    gender  = factor(if_else(female == 1, "Women", "Men")),
    college = as.integer(grade92 >= 43),
    edu_cat = factor(
      case_when(grade92 < 43 ~ "No degree",
                grade92 == 43 ~ "Bachelor",
                TRUE ~ "Graduate"),
      levels = c("No degree", "Bachelor", "Graduate")
    )
  )
glimpse(cps)
```

The data contain `r nrow(cps)` market research analysts, `r sum(cps$female)`
of them women. `earnwke` are weekly earnings in USD, `uhours` usual weekly
hours.

---

# Part 1: Simple regression in six steps

## 1.1 Question and exploration

**Question:** How are weekly earnings related to age?

```{r}
#| label: scatter

ggplot(cps, aes(x = age, y = earnwke)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Weekly earnings (USD)")
```

```{r}
#| label: ceiling

max(cps$earnwke)
sum(cps$earnwke == max(cps$earnwke))
```

The relationship is positive but weak and noisy. Earnings stop at
`r fmt(max(cps$earnwke))` USD: the CPS top-codes high earnings, and
`r sum(cps$earnwke == max(cps$earnwke))` analysts sit at this ceiling.

```{r}
#| label: histograms
#| fig-height: 3.5

ggplot(cps, aes(x = earnwke)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25) +
  labs(x = "Weekly earnings (USD)")

ggplot(cps, aes(x = log(earnwke))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25) +
  labs(x = "ln(weekly earnings)")
```

Earnings are right-skewed; in logs, the distribution is more symmetric
(not perfectly: now the left tail is longer, and the ceiling is still visible).

## 1.2 Specify and estimate

```{r}
#| label: slr

m1 <- lm(earnwke ~ age, data = cps)
summary(m1)
```

```{r}
#| label: slr-tidy

tidy(m1, conf.int = TRUE)
glance(m1)$r.squared
```

- **Slope:** `r fmt(coef(m1)[["age"]], 1)` — analysts who are one year
  older earn, *on average*, about 14 USD more per week. This compares
  people of different ages; it is neither causal nor about any individual.
- **Standard error:** `r fmt(tidy(m1)$std.error[2], 1)`, **95% CI:**
  [`r fmt(confint(m1)["age", 1], 1)`, `r fmt(confint(m1)["age", 2], 1)`],
  t ≈ `r fmt(tidy(m1)$statistic[2], 1)` — the slope is clearly different
  from zero.
- **R²:** `r fmt(glance(m1)$r.squared, 3)` — age alone describes little of
  the variation in earnings. This says nothing about whether the slope is
  right, and nothing about how well we would predict new analysts.

## 1.3 Diagnose

`augment()` adds fitted values (`.fitted`) and residuals (`.resid`) to the
data.

```{r}
#| label: slr-diagnose

augment(m1) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Fitted values", y = "Residuals")
```

The residuals show a hump: the straight line is too low in the middle and too
high at both ends. Back to exploring and specifying.

## 1.4 Back to the data: age²

```{r}
#| label: smoother

ggplot(cps, aes(x = age, y = earnwke)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, colour = "darkgreen") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x + I(x^2), se = FALSE, colour = "red") +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Weekly earnings (USD)")
```

`I(age^2)` adds the square of age as a second variable. The model is still
linear in the parameters, so `lm()` fits it as before.

```{r}
#| label: quadratic

m2 <- lm(earnwke ~ age + I(age^2), data = cps)
tidy(m2)
glance(m2)$r.squared
```

```{r}
#| label: quadratic-diagnose

augment(m2) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Fitted values", y = "Residuals")
```

The hump has left the residuals. The diagonal stripe at the top right are the
top-coded analysts.

## 1.5 Interpret the curve

With age², the slope depends on age: $\hat\beta_1 + 2\hat\beta_2 \cdot a$.

```{r}
#| label: slope-at-age

b <- coef(m2)
slope_at <- function(a) b[["age"]] + 2 * b[["I(age^2)"]] * a
slope_at(c(30, 45, 60))
-b[["age"]] / (2 * b[["I(age^2)"]])   # age with the highest predicted earnings
```

About +42 USD per year at 30, +7 at 45 and −27 at 60; predicted earnings
peak at about 48 years. The coefficient 110.2 on its own is the slope at age
0 — meaningless here.

## 1.6 Logs

```{r}
#| label: log-model

m_log <- lm(log(earnwke) ~ age, data = cps)
tidy(m_log)
```

In a log–level model, $100 \cdot \hat\beta$ is (approximately) the percentage
change: one year of age goes with about
`r fmt(100 * coef(m_log)[["age"]], 1)` % higher earnings.

---

# Part 2: Multiple regression

**Question:** Do women earn less?

## 2.1 The raw gap

```{r}
#| label: group-means

cps |>
  group_by(gender) |>
  summarise(n = n(), earnings = mean(earnwke), hours = mean(uhours))
```

```{r}
#| label: raw-gap

m_gap <- lm(earnwke ~ female, data = cps)
tidy(m_gap)
```

The coefficient of a 0/1 variable is the difference in means:
`r fmt(coef(m_gap)[["female"]])` USD. The intercept is the mean of the men.
But women also work fewer hours.

## 2.2 Holding hours constant

```{r}
#| label: gap-hours

m_hours <- lm(earnwke ~ female + uhours, data = cps)
tidy(m_hours)
```

Among analysts working the same hours, the gap shrinks to
`r fmt(coef(m_hours)[["female"]])` USD — and with a standard error of
`r fmt(tidy(m_hours)$std.error[2])` it can no longer be told apart from zero.

Where did the other 150 USD go? Women work fewer hours, and hours pay:

```{r}
#| label: decomposition

delta <- coef(lm(uhours ~ female, data = cps))[["female"]]
delta

coef(m_hours)[["female"]] + coef(m_hours)[["uhours"]] * delta  # = the raw gap
```

Total gap = direct gap + (effect of hours × hours gap):
−218 = −69 + 40.9 × (−3.66). Which of the two numbers answers "Do women
earn less?" depends on the question: the **total** effect (−218) includes
the path via hours; the **direct** effect (−69) compares equal hours. If
fewer hours are themselves a result of norms or penalties, controlling for
them removes part of what we want to measure.

## 2.3 Model (3): more controls

```{r}
#| label: model-3

m3 <- lm(earnwke ~ female + age + I(age^2) + uhours + college, data = cps)
tidy(m3, conf.int = TRUE)
glance(m3) |> select(r.squared, adj.r.squared)
```

Side by side:

```{r}
#| label: compare-gap

list(`(1) raw` = m_gap, `(2) + hours` = m_hours, `(3) + age, age², college` = m3) |>
  map_dfr(\(m) tidy(m) |> filter(term == "female"), .id = "model") |>
  select(model, estimate, std.error)
```

## 2.4 Diagnose model (3) — and a better-behaved model (4)

```{r}
#| label: diagnose-3
#| fig-height: 3.5

d3 <- augment(m3)
ggplot(d3, aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE)

ggplot(d3, aes(sample = .resid)) +
  stat_qq() +
  stat_qq_line()
```

The Q-Q plot shows a heavy right tail. Logs help — for earnings, and for
hours:

```{r}
#| label: model-4

m4 <- lm(log(earnwke) ~ female + age + I(age^2) + log(uhours) + college, data = cps)
tidy(m4)
glance(m4)$r.squared
```

```{r}
#| label: diagnose-4
#| fig-height: 3.5

ggplot(augment(m4), aes(sample = .resid)) +
  stat_qq() +
  stat_qq_line()
```

- The residuals are now close to normal; R² rises from
  `r fmt(glance(m3)$r.squared, 2)` to `r fmt(glance(m4)$r.squared, 2)`.
- **Gap:** `r fmt(coef(m4)[["female"]], 3)` → about
  `r fmt(100 * (exp(coef(m4)[["female"]]) - 1))` % (exact:
  $e^{\hat\beta} - 1$), again not distinguishable from zero.
- **Hours** (log–log): an elasticity of
  `r fmt(coef(m4)[["log(uhours)"]], 2)` — 1 % more hours go with about
  1.3 % higher earnings.

---

# Part 3: Groups and interactions

## 3.1 Categories with more levels

```{r}
#| label: education

table(cps$edu_cat)

m_edu <- lm(earnwke ~ female + age + I(age^2) + uhours + edu_cat, data = cps)
tidy(m_edu)
```

R uses the first level of a factor as the reference group: here "No degree".
Bachelor's: +`r fmt(coef(m_edu)[["edu_catBachelor"]])` USD, graduate
degree: +`r fmt(coef(m_edu)[["edu_catGraduate"]])` USD, each compared with
analysts without a degree. To compare with Bachelor's instead:

```{r}
#| label: relevel

cps_b <- cps |> mutate(edu_cat = relevel(edu_cat, ref = "Bachelor"))
lm(earnwke ~ female + age + I(age^2) + uhours + edu_cat, data = cps_b) |>
  tidy()
```

Same model, same fit — only the comparisons in the table change. Graduate vs
Bachelor's: about +285 USD.

## 3.2 Parallel slopes vs interaction model

```{r}
#| label: par-int

m_par <- lm(earnwke ~ age + female, data = cps)
m_int <- lm(earnwke ~ age * female, data = cps)  # = age + female + age:female
tidy(m_par)
tidy(m_int)
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-par-int
#| fig-height: 3.5

bind_rows(
  augment(m_par, data = cps) |> mutate(model = "Parallel slopes"),
  augment(m_int, data = cps) |> mutate(model = "Interaction")
) |>
  mutate(model = fct_inorder(model)) |>  # panels in this order, not alphabetical
  ggplot(aes(x = age, colour = gender)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = earnwke), alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(aes(y = .fitted), linewidth = 1.2) +
  facet_wrap(~model) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Weekly earnings (USD)", colour = NULL)
```

- Men: slope `r fmt(coef(m_int)[["age"]], 1)`; women:
  `r fmt(coef(m_int)[["age"]] + coef(m_int)[["age:female"]], 1)`; the
  difference (`r fmt(coef(m_int)[["age:female"]], 1)`, SE
  `r fmt(tidy(m_int)$std.error[4], 1)`) is not precisely estimated.
- `female` = `r fmt(coef(m_int)[["female"]], 1)` is the gap at age **0** —
  not "the" gap.

## 3.3 Centring

Measure age from 40 instead of from 0:

```{r}
#| label: centring

m_int40 <- lm(earnwke ~ I(age - 40) * female, data = cps)
tidy(m_int40)
```

Same model, same fit; `female` is now the gap at age 40:
`r fmt(coef(m_int40)[["female"]])` USD.

## 3.4 Plot the gap instead of reading coefficients

Centring at each age in turn gives the gap at that age, with its
confidence interval:

```{r}
#| label: gap-by-age

gap_by_age <- map_dfr(seq(25, 60, by = 5), \(a) {
  lm(earnwke ~ I(age - a) * female, data = cps) |>
    tidy(conf.int = TRUE) |>
    filter(term == "female") |>
    mutate(age = a)
})

ggplot(gap_by_age, aes(x = age, y = estimate)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Predicted gap, women − men (USD)")
```

The gap widens with age, but the band is wide: at young ages it includes
zero.

---

# Summary: the running example in six steps

| Step | What we did |
|:--|:--|
| **Question** | Do earnings rise with age? Do women earn less — and why? |
| **Explore** | Weak, hump-shaped age profile · skew · ceiling · women work fewer hours |
| **Specify** | Age² · logs · hours: total or direct effect? · interaction age × female |
| **Estimate** | `lm()` · slope 14.4 · gap −218 raw, −69 to −83 with controls, ≈ −5 % in logs |
| **Diagnose** | `augment()`: hump → age² · heavy right tail → logs · top-coding |
| **Interpret** | Gap mostly linked to hours · not causal · imprecise with n = 252 |
